body_markdown:
## Why Streamlit?

You have written scripts and notebooks that do clever things — but a recruiter cannot run a `.py` file. **Streamlit** turns a plain Python script into a web app you can share with a link. No HTML, CSS, or JavaScript needed: you write Python, Streamlit draws the page.

For an AI portfolio this is gold. A working, clickable app that calls a model is far more persuasive than a screenshot.

## Install and run

Streamlit installs with pip. You launch an app with the `streamlit run` command — not plain `python`.

```bash
pip install streamlit
streamlit run app.py
```

This opens your app in the browser, usually at http://localhost:8501, and reloads automatically when you save the file.

## Display and input

Every widget is a function. `st.write` shows almost anything; `st.dataframe` shows a table; input widgets return the user's value.

```python
import streamlit as st

st.title("My first app")
name = st.text_input("Your name")
if st.button("Greet"):
    st.write(f"Hello, {name}!")
```

## The rerun model

Here is the one idea that confuses everyone: **every interaction reruns the whole script from top to bottom**. A button click, a slider drag — the entire file runs again. To remember values between runs, use `st.session_state`, a dictionary that survives reruns.

```python
if "count" not in st.session_state:
    st.session_state.count = 0
if st.button("Add one"):
    st.session_state.count += 1
st.write("Count:", st.session_state.count)
```

## Calling Claude from your app

Keep your key in an environment variable (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`) or `.streamlit/secrets.toml` — never in the code. Because the script reruns often, wrap slow or paid work carefully and only call the model on a button press.

```python
import streamlit as st
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()
prompt = st.text_area("Ask Claude")
if st.button("Send"):
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=1024,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    )
    st.write(msg.content[0].text)
```

## Cache the slow parts

Loading a big CSV or computing a chart on every rerun is wasteful. Decorate the function with `@st.cache_data` and Streamlit reuses the result when inputs do not change.

```python
@st.cache_data
def load_data(path):
    return pd.read_csv(path)
```

## Your task

Take a script from an earlier lesson and **wrap it in a Streamlit app** with at least one input widget and one output. Bonus: deploy it free on Streamlit Community Cloud.

slides.narration: Getting started takes two commands. First, pip install streamlit. Then, and this is the part people forget, you launch the app with streamlit run app dot py, not with plain python. It opens in your browser at localhost port eighty-five-oh-one, and it reloads automatically every time you save. That fast feedback loop makes building genuinely fun.

slides.title: Show things on screen
bullets: st.title and st.write for text.
st.dataframe for interactive tables.
st.line_chart for quick charts.
Each element is just a function call.
slides.code:
import streamlit as st
st.title("My app")
st.write("Hello!")
st.line_chart(data)
slides.narration: Putting things on the page is simple: every element is a function. st dot title gives you a heading. st dot write shows almost anything you pass it, from text to numbers. st dot dataframe renders an interactive sortable table, and st dot line chart draws a chart from your data in one line. You think in Python and Streamlit handles the layout.

slides.title: Collect user input
bullets: Widgets return the user's value.
st.text_input, st.slider, st.button.
Store the return value in a variable.
Use it like any normal Python value.
slides.narration: Input widgets are also functions, and each one returns the value the user entered. st dot text input gives back the typed text, st dot slider gives back a number, and st dot button returns true on the run where it was clicked. You capture that value in a variable and use it like any other Python value. Here we greet the user only when the button is pressed.

slides.title: The rerun model
bullets: Every interaction reruns the whole script.
Top to bottom, every single time.
Simple to reason about once you know it.
This is the key Streamlit idea.
slides.narration: Here's the one concept that confuses everyone, so listen closely. Every time a user interacts, a click, a slider drag, anything, Streamlit reruns your entire script from top to bottom. The whole file runs again. It sounds wasteful, but it makes apps wonderfully simple to reason about. Once this clicks, everything else in Streamlit makes sense.

slides.title: Remember with session_state
bullets: Reruns wipe normal variables.
st.session_state survives reruns.
Works like a dictionary.
Initialise it before you use it.
slides.narration: Because the script reruns every time, ordinary variables reset on each interaction. To remember something, like a counter or a chat history, you use st dot session state. It behaves like a dictionary that survives reruns for that user's session. The pattern is: check if the key exists, set a default if not, then update it. Now your counter actually counts up.

slides.title: Call Claude from your app
bullets: Keep the key in an env var or secrets.
Never hard-code A P I keys.
Call the model on a button press only.
Show msg.content[0].text as the reply.
slides.code:
from anthropic import Anthropic
client = Anthropic()
if st.button("Send"):
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=1024,
        messages=[{"role":"user","content":prompt}])
    st.write(msg.content[0].text)
slides.narration: Now the fun part: wiring in Claude. We create an Anthropic client, which reads your key from the ANTHROPIC A P I KEY environment variable. Keep that key in an env var or a secrets file, never in the code, so it never lands on GitHub. Because the script reruns so often, we only call the model inside the button block, then show the reply from msg dot content, index zero, dot text.

slides.title: Keep it fast with caching
bullets: Slow work repeats on every rerun.
Decorate with @st.cache_data.
Same inputs return instantly.
Great for loading data or files.
slides.narration: Since the whole script reruns constantly, slow work like reading a big C S V would repeat every single time. The fix is caching. Put the at sign st dot cache data decorator above a function, and Streamlit stores its result. Next time you call it with the same inputs, it returns instantly instead of redoing the work. Your app stays snappy even with heavy data.
